guides.title: Professional requests
guides.explanation: At work, we don't give orders. We ask. Use 'Could you…?' or 'Can you…?' and add 'please'. For a bigger request, use 'Would it be possible to…?'
expressions: Could you please send me…?
Can you help me with…?
Would it be possible to…?
Please send it by Friday.
I'll send it by Thursday.
Thanks for your help.

vocabulary.gloss: the last day or time to finish something
new information about your work
a plan with days and times
a document about work or results

examples.label: Too direct
examples.text: Send me the file.

examples.label: Better
examples.text: Could you please send me the file?

examples.label: Bigger request
examples.text: Would it be possible to send me the file today?

mistake.wrong: I will send it until 4.
mistake.right: I will send it by 4.
mistake.why: 'By 4' means 'at 4 or before'. 'Until' is for things that continue, like 'I work until 6'.

guides.tip: Ask for one thing in each email. Two requests in one email are easy to forget.

guides.title: Disagreeing politely
guides.explanation: Professional disagreement in English follows a pattern: acknowledge, then pivot, then propose. Going straight to 'no' reads as aggressive, even when you are right.
expressions: I see your point, but…
I'm not sure I agree, because…
That's a fair point — my concern is…
I'd look at it slightly differently.
I agree in principle, though I wonder whether…

vocabulary.gloss: a worry you can explain with a reason
what you lose in order to gain something else
another option
the reasoning behind a decision

examples.label: Too blunt
examples.text: No, that won't work.

examples.label: Better
examples.text: I see the logic, but I'm concerned it won't work with the current timeline.

examples.label: Best — adds an option
examples.text: I see the logic. My concern is the timeline. Could we phase it instead?

mistake.wrong: I am not agree.
mistake.right: I don't agree. / I disagree.
mistake.why: 'Agree' is a verb in English, not an adjective. No 'be' before it.

guides.tip: Disagree with the idea, never with the person: 'that approach' rather than 'your approach'.

guides.title: Giving opinions
guides.explanation: A good opinion has two parts: what you think and why. Start with 'I think…' or 'In my opinion…', then give a reason with 'because'. To agree, say 'I agree' and add something.
expressions: I think…
In my opinion…
I agree with you.
I don't agree, because…
That's a good idea.
I think so too.

vocabulary.gloss: what you think about something
why you think something
to think the same
to think differently

examples.label: Opinion only
examples.text: I think we should wait.

examples.label: Opinion + reason
examples.text: I think we should wait, because the numbers are not ready.

examples.label: Agreeing
examples.text: I agree with Yusuf. The price is the main problem.

mistake.wrong: According to me, the plan is good.
mistake.right: In my opinion, the plan is good.
mistake.why: 'According to' is for other people: 'according to the report'. For you, say 'in my opinion' or 'I think'.

guides.tip: Always say 'because'. A reason makes your opinion stronger.

guides.title: Suggestions and advice
guides.explanation: A suggestion is an idea for the group: 'Let's…', 'Shall we…?', 'How about…?'. Advice is for one person: 'You should…'. Suggestions sound friendly because they are open.
expressions: Let's take a short break.
Shall we start?
How about meeting on Friday?
Why don't we ask Elena?
We could send it tomorrow.
You should talk to your manager.

vocabulary.gloss: something you think of
one possible choice
a short rest
what you think another person should do

examples.label: Suggestion
examples.text: How about moving the launch to next week?

examples.label: Suggestion
examples.text: Let's ask the client first.

examples.label: Advice
examples.text: You should call the supplier today.

mistake.wrong: You should to call him.
mistake.right: You should call him.
mistake.why: After 'should', use the base verb. No 'to'.

guides.tip: 'How about…?' opens a discussion. 'You should…' gives an answer. Choose the one you need.

guides.title: Apologising at work
guides.explanation: A good work apology is short. Say sorry once, say what went wrong, then say what you will do now. Don't write a long, emotional apology.
expressions: I'm sorry for the delay.
Sorry, that was my mistake.
I apologise for the problem.
Thank you for waiting.
I'll send it today.
It won't happen again.

vocabulary.gloss: when something is late
something done wrong
to repair or correct something
waiting calmly, without getting angry

examples.label: Too short
examples.text: Sorry!

examples.label: Too much
examples.text: I'm so, so sorry, I feel terrible, it was a very bad week…

examples.label: Good
examples.text: I'm sorry for the delay. The report is attached now.

mistake.wrong: I apologise you for the delay.
mistake.right: I apologise for the delay.
mistake.why: Say 'apologise for' something. Don't put a person right after 'apologise'.

guides.tip: Say sorry in one sentence. Then talk about the solution.

guides.title: Asking for clarification
guides.explanation: It's normal not to understand everything. Ask a short, polite question. You can ask someone to repeat, to spell a word, or to explain one thing. After 'Could you tell me…', use normal word order. Say 'where the room is', not 'where is the room'.
expressions: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?
Could you speak more slowly, please?
How do you spell that?
What do you mean by…?
Do you mean Monday or Tuesday?
Could you tell me where the meeting is?

vocabulary.gloss: to say something again
to say the letters of a word
to make something clear
information about how to do something

examples.label: Too short
examples.text: What?

examples.label: Better
examples.text: Sorry, could you repeat the date, please?

examples.label: Best: give two choices
examples.text: Do you mean this Friday or next Friday?

mistake.wrong: Can you explain me the process?
mistake.right: Can you explain the process to me?
mistake.why: Say 'explain something to someone'. Don't put 'me' right after 'explain'.

guides.tip: Give two choices in your question: 'Friday or Monday?' It is fast and easy to answer.

guides.title: Negotiating
guides.explanation: Negotiation language in English is conditional. You rarely say what you want directly; you say what becomes possible if something else changes.
expressions: If we could…, then we'd be able to…
Would you be open to…?
That works for me, provided that…
I can do X if Y moves.
Where's the flexibility on your side?
Based on the market rate for this role, I'm looking at…

vocabulary.gloss: fixed money paid for a job
salary plus all other benefits
room to change the terms
a different offer made in response
the amount of work included

examples.label: Demanding
examples.text: I need more money.

examples.label: Better
examples.text: Based on the responsibilities in this role, I'm looking at the 55–60k range.

examples.label: Trading
examples.text: I could work with 52k if there's a review at six months.

mistake.wrong: I want that you pay more.
mistake.right: I'd like you to review the figure.
mistake.why: 'Want' is not followed by 'that' + clause. Use 'want someone to do', and at work, prefer 'I'd like'.

guides.tip: Never name the first number without a reason attached to it. The reason is what makes it negotiable rather than emotional.

guides.title: Explaining problems
guides.explanation: The professional order is: what happened, what the impact is, what you are doing, what you need. Starting with the excuse loses the room.
expressions: The issue is that…
What happened was…
As a result…
The impact is…
Here's what I've done so far:
What I need from you is…

vocabulary.gloss: a problem, said neutrally
the real reason underneath
a temporary fix
to move a problem to someone more senior
time when a system is not working

examples.label: Excuse first
examples.text: It wasn't my fault — the supplier was late and nobody told me…

examples.label: Better
examples.text: The delivery is two days late. That pushes testing to Thursday. I've asked the supplier for a firm date and I'll confirm by 2 p.m.

mistake.wrong: The problem is happened yesterday.
mistake.right: The problem happened yesterday.
mistake.why: 'Happen' is not passive and takes no 'be'.

guides.tip: Bad news travels best early and short. One paragraph beats a long apology sent late.

guides.title: Giving and receiving feedback
guides.explanation: Useful feedback is about observable work, not personality. When receiving it, the professional move is to ask one clarifying question before responding.
expressions: One thing that worked really well is…
I'd suggest changing…
Have you thought about…?
What would make this stronger is…
Thank you — that's useful.
Could you give me an example?
Let me take that away and come back to you.

vocabulary.gloss: intended to help improve
a changed version
an early version
what someone is good at
what someone needs to improve

examples.label: About the person
examples.text: You're careless with details.

examples.label: About the work
examples.text: There are three figures in the table that don't match the appendix.

examples.label: Receiving well
examples.text: Thank you — could you point me to the section you mean?

mistake.wrong: You did a mistake in the report.
mistake.right: You made a mistake in the report.
mistake.why: In English you MAKE a mistake and DO a task.

guides.tip: Never defend in the same minute you receive feedback. 'Let me look at that and come back to you' buys you a day and costs you nothing.

guides.title: Meeting language
guides.explanation: Meetings have their own small set of verbal signals: entering the conversation, holding the floor, and closing. Learn the signals and you can participate at a level above your grammar.
expressions: Sorry, can I just add something?
Could I come in on that point?
Just to build on what Marta said…
Can I check one thing before we move on?
So, to summarise…
The actions are: …
Shall we take that offline?

vocabulary.gloss: the list of items for the meeting
the written record of a meeting
a task someone agreed to do
to lead a meeting
outside this meeting

examples.label: Interrupting badly
examples.text: No, listen —

examples.label: Interrupting well
examples.text: Sorry to jump in — can I add one thing on the budget?

examples.label: Closing
examples.text: To summarise: Ana sends the draft Tuesday, I review by Thursday, we decide Friday.

mistake.wrong: I want to say something for the budget.
mistake.right: I'd like to say something about the budget.
mistake.why: You speak ABOUT or ON a topic, not 'for' it.

guides.tip: Say the person's name before you disagree with them. It turns an attack into a conversation.

guides.title: Small talk at work
guides.explanation: Small talk is a short, friendly chat. It helps people work well together. Keep it short and positive, and ask questions about the other person. When you thank someone, say what they did.
expressions: How's your week going?
How was your weekend?
Nice to meet you.
What do you do?
Thanks so much for your help.
It was nice talking to you.

vocabulary.gloss: a person you work with
to talk in a friendly way
to say thank you
a big event with talks, often in another city

examples.label: Too short
examples.text: Thanks.

examples.label: Better
examples.text: Thanks for your help yesterday.

examples.label: Best: say what they did
examples.text: Thanks for staying late yesterday. We finished on time because of you.

mistake.wrong: How do you do your work?
mistake.right: What do you do? / How's work?
mistake.why: 'How do you do?' is only a very formal greeting. It is not a real question about work.

guides.tip: When you say thank you, say what the person did. It means much more.

guides.title: Saying no professionally
guides.explanation: A professional 'no' is never just 'no'. It contains a reason, an alternative, or a condition, which is why it rarely damages the relationship.
expressions: I'd like to help, but I'm at capacity this week.
I can't take that on by Friday — I could do Tuesday.
That's not something I can commit to right now.
If X moves, I can do Y.
Let me check what I can realistically do.

vocabulary.gloss: how much work you can actually take
informal word for available time and energy
to promise firmly
to change the order of what matters

examples.label: Unclear
examples.text: I'll try.

examples.label: Clear no
examples.text: I can't do Friday. I can have it to you Tuesday morning.

examples.label: Conditional no
examples.text: I can take that on if the Ortiz report moves to next week. Which would you prefer?

mistake.wrong: I have not time.
mistake.right: I don't have time. / I haven't got time.
mistake.why: 'Have' as a main verb needs 'do' to make the negative.

guides.tip: Give your no a date. 'No' plus a real alternative date is heard as commitment, not refusal.

guides.title: Professional tone
guides.explanation: Tone in English is carried by structure more than by vocabulary. Bare imperatives and flat negatives read as cold; questions, modals, a named person and a brief acknowledgement read as warm, with identical information. At this level the skill is calibration: firm without being curt, warm without being servile, and never passive-aggressive.
expressions: Would you mind…?
When you get a chance…
I'd be grateful if…
I appreciate this isn't what you were hoping to hear.
To be clear, the date can't move.
Thanks for picking this up.

vocabulary.gloss: how formal or informal language is
so short it seems rude
polite in a professional way
short and complete
polite on the surface, hostile underneath ('Per my previous email…')

examples.label: Cold
examples.text: Need this today.

examples.label: Neutral
examples.text: Could I have this today?

examples.label: Warm and still clear
examples.text: Hi Tomás — any chance of this today? Happy to help if it's tight.

mistake.wrong: Dear Sir, hey, so about the thing…
mistake.right: Hi Ana, quick question about the Q3 report…
mistake.why: Mixing registers is worse than choosing the wrong one. Pick a level and stay there.

guides.tip: Read your message out loud. If you would not say it to the person's face, rewrite it.

guides.title: Softening and hedging
guides.explanation: English uses hedging words to leave room for the other person to disagree. Too few and you sound aggressive; too many and you sound like you do not believe yourself.
expressions: It seems that…
I'd say it's probably…
There may be a risk that…
slightly / a little / a bit
I might be missing something, but…
Correct me if I'm wrong, but…

vocabulary.gloss: to make a statement less absolute
not final, open to change
clear and confident without being aggressive

examples.label: Too hard
examples.text: This is wrong.

examples.label: Hedged
examples.text: I think there may be an error in the second column.

examples.label: Too soft — avoid
examples.text: I'm really sorry, this is probably just me, but maybe possibly there might perhaps be a small issue?

mistake.wrong: Maybe perhaps possibly we could potentially…
mistake.right: We could possibly…
mistake.why: One hedge is enough. Stacking them destroys your authority.

guides.tip: Hedge the claim, never the commitment. 'It may be Thursday' is fine; 'I may send it Thursday' is not.

guides.title: Structuring an email
guides.explanation: A work email has a simple shape: a greeting, why you are writing, the details, what you need and when, and a closing. Put the most important thing near the top.
expressions: Dear Ms Lemoine, (formal)
Hi Marc, (a colleague)
I'm writing to ask about…
Please find attached…
Could you reply by Thursday?
Kind regards, / Best regards,

vocabulary.gloss: the title of the email
a file you send with an email
to send a copy to another person
the words at the end, like 'Kind regards'

examples.label: Bad subject
examples.text: Question

examples.label: Good subject
examples.text: Q3 report: figures needed by Thursday

examples.label: Good first line
examples.text: Hi Marcus, I'm writing about the Q3 report.

mistake.wrong: I am writing you for ask about the report.
mistake.right: I'm writing to ask about the report.
mistake.why: Use 'to' + verb to say why you are writing: 'writing to ask', 'writing to confirm'.

guides.tip: Put the day you need an answer in the subject line. Everyone reads the subject line.

guides.title: Async and chat writing
guides.explanation: Chat and async updates are read fast, often on a phone, often by someone eight hours behind you. Front-load the point and make the ask unmissable.
expressions: Heads-up:
No rush, but…
Blocked on:
Need a decision by EOD.
Context in thread ↓
Copying you for visibility.

vocabulary.gloss: not at the same time
end of day
something stopping you making progress
a short daily team update
a chain of connected messages
the local time where someone is

examples.label: Hard to act on
examples.text: Hey! When you have time could we maybe talk about the thing from yesterday?

examples.label: Better
examples.text: Need a yes/no on the Vidal quote by EOD your time — details in thread.

mistake.wrong: Hi. / Hello? / Are you there?
mistake.right: Hi Ana — quick question about the Vidal quote: can we approve 4.2k?
mistake.why: Never send a greeting alone. It makes the other person wait to find out what you want.

guides.tip: Write the update so someone can act on it without asking you a single follow-up question.

guides.title: Report writing
guides.explanation: A report is read by people with no time and no context. The first paragraph must survive alone: what happened, what it means, what you recommend.
expressions: This report covers…
The main finding is…
Overall, …
The data suggests that…
We recommend that…
Further work is needed on…

vocabulary.gloss: what you discovered
what you advise doing
the short version
extra detail at the end
what the report does and does not cover

examples.label: Buried conclusion
examples.text: First we gathered data, then we analysed it, then… therefore we recommend X.

examples.label: Better
examples.text: We recommend option B. This report sets out the two options, the cost of each, and the reasoning.

mistake.wrong: In this report I will talk about many things.
mistake.right: This report covers the two supplier options and recommends one.
mistake.why: Reports state their conclusion. They do not build suspense.

guides.tip: Write the summary last, then move it to the top.

guides.title: Linking expressions
guides.explanation: Linking words are what turn a list of sentences into an argument. At B1 they are also the fastest way to sound more advanced than your grammar.
expressions: Adding: moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides
Contrasting: however, although, on the other hand, whereas
Examples: for example, for instance, such as
Result: as a result, therefore, consequently
Concluding: in conclusion, overall, to sum up

vocabulary.gloss: introduces a contrast; needs a comma
joins two clauses in one sentence
compares two different facts
introduces a logical result

examples.label: No linking
examples.text: Public transport is cheap. Cars are comfortable.

examples.label: Contrast
examples.text: Public transport is cheaper. On the other hand, cars are more comfortable.

examples.label: Concession
examples.text: Although he was tired, he continued working.

mistake.wrong: Although it was expensive, but we bought it.
mistake.right: Although it was expensive, we bought it.
mistake.why: 'Although' and 'but' do the same job. Use one, never both.

guides.tip: Three linkers in a paragraph is plenty. More than that and it reads like a grammar exercise.

guides.title: Tenses at work
guides.explanation: Most work English uses three tenses. Present simple for habits (We meet every Monday). Present continuous for now (I'm working on it). Past simple for finished actions (We sent it yesterday).
expressions: We usually meet on Mondays. (habit)
I'm writing the report now. (now)
She's working from home today. (now)
I finished the project last month. (finished)
We sent the invoice yesterday. (finished)

vocabulary.gloss: something you do regularly
now
time words that need the past simple
a piece of work with a goal and an end

examples.label: Habit
examples.text: The team meets every Monday at nine.

examples.label: Now
examples.text: She's talking to a client at the moment.

examples.label: Finished
examples.text: We launched the website last March.

mistake.wrong: I have finished it yesterday.
mistake.right: I finished it yesterday.
mistake.why: With 'yesterday', 'last week' or a date, use the past simple.

guides.tip: Look for time words. 'Every day' means present simple. 'Now' means present continuous. 'Yesterday' means past simple.

guides.title: Present perfect at work
guides.explanation: The present perfect connects the past to now. At work it does three jobs: reporting completed work without saying when, describing experience, and explaining a current situation caused by a past action.
expressions: I've sent the report. (it's done, it matters now)
I've already spoken to the supplier.
We haven't heard back yet.
I've worked in marketing for six years.
Have you had a chance to look at it?

vocabulary.gloss: sooner than expected
up to now — in questions and negatives
continuing, often with surprise
from a point in time
across a length of time

examples.label: Result now
examples.text: I've finished the draft — it's in your inbox.

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: I've managed teams of up to twelve people.

examples.label: Not yet
examples.text: We still haven't received their confirmation.

mistake.wrong: I have sent it yesterday.
mistake.right: I sent it yesterday.
mistake.why: A finished time expression forces the past simple. Present perfect never takes 'yesterday', 'last week' or a date.

guides.tip: In status updates, present perfect is your best friend: 'I've spoken to…, I've updated…, I haven't heard back on…'

guides.title: Future forms at work
guides.explanation: English has three common ways to talk about the future. Use 'going to' for plans you already have. Use the present continuous (I'm meeting) for things in your calendar. Use 'will' for decisions you make now and for promises.
expressions: I'm going to call the client today. (plan)
I'm meeting Ana on Tuesday. (calendar)
I'll send it now. (decision now)
Don't worry, I'll help you. (promise)
I think it will be busy. (opinion)

vocabulary.gloss: something you decided to do
a meeting or event in your calendar
when you say you will do something
where you write your meetings and dates

examples.label: Plan
examples.text: We're going to open a new office in May.

examples.label: Calendar
examples.text: I'm presenting on Wednesday morning.

examples.label: Decision now
examples.text: The room is busy? OK, I'll book another one.

mistake.wrong: I'm going to meeting the client.
mistake.right: I'm going to meet the client.
mistake.why: After 'going to', use the base verb: 'going to meet', 'going to call'.

guides.tip: In a meeting, 'I'll do it' is a promise. People will remember it.

guides.title: Modal verbs at work
guides.explanation: Modals carry the social weight of workplace English. They turn facts into advice, obligation, possibility or requests, without changing any other word in the sentence.
expressions: You should…  (advice)
We must / have to…  (obligation)
It might / may…  (possibility)
Could you…?  (request)
We could…  (option)
You don't have to…  (no obligation)

vocabulary.gloss: something required
something that may happen
being allowed
strong advice

examples.label: Advice
examples.text: You should copy Legal on that.

examples.label: Possibility
examples.text: The client might ask for a discount.

examples.label: Obligation
examples.text: We have to submit it before the 30th.

mistake.wrong: You must to send it today.
mistake.right: You must send it today.
mistake.why: Modals are followed by the bare infinitive: never 'to'. Exception: 'have to', 'ought to'.

guides.tip: 'Must' from a colleague sounds like an order. Use 'we need to' or 'we have to' unless you are the one setting the rule.

guides.title: Conditionals at work
guides.explanation: The first conditional talks about real future possibilities. Deadlines, risks, plans. The second talks about hypothetical or unlikely ones. Useful for advice and for negotiating without committing.
expressions: If we start Monday, we'll finish by the 14th. (real)
If the client agrees, we can begin. (real)
If I were you, I'd raise it now. (advice)
If we had more budget, we'd hire a freelancer. (hypothetical)
Unless we hear back today, we'll proceed.

vocabulary.gloss: what must be true first
what results
if not
only if

examples.label: First conditional
examples.text: If people recycle more, pollution will decrease.

examples.label: Second conditional
examples.text: If I had more time, I would redo the analysis.

examples.label: Advice
examples.text: If I were you, I would exercise more.

mistake.wrong: If we will start Monday, we finish by the 14th.
mistake.right: If we start Monday, we'll finish by the 14th.
mistake.why: No 'will' in the 'if' half. Present simple in the condition, 'will' in the result.

guides.tip: Second conditional is the safest way to negotiate: 'If we could move the date, I'd be able to…' commits to nothing.

guides.title: Passive voice and reported speech
guides.explanation: The passive moves focus from who did something to what was done. Essential in reports and incident write-ups. Reported speech lets you carry someone else's words into a new conversation accurately.
expressions: The invoice was sent on Monday.
A decision has been made.
The system is being upgraded.
She said that she was tired.
He told me the deadline had moved.
They asked whether we could deliver earlier.

vocabulary.gloss: the action matters more than the doer
to say what someone else said
who is responsible

examples.label: Active
examples.text: Marta approved the budget.

examples.label: Passive — neutral
examples.text: The budget was approved on 3 March.

examples.label: Reported
examples.text: She said the budget had been approved.

mistake.wrong: She said me that she will come.
mistake.right: She told me that she would come. / She said that she would come.
mistake.why: 'Tell' takes a person, 'say' does not. And the tense shifts back one step.

guides.tip: Use the passive when naming the person would start an argument. Use the active when you want credit or accountability to be clear.

guides.title: Comparing options
guides.explanation: Decisions at work are almost always comparisons. The grammar is simple; the skill at this level is scale and judgement: how much better, at what cost, and which option you would actually choose.
expressions: A is marginally / considerably cheaper than B.
A is by far the most reliable of the three.
A is not quite as fast as B.
Compared with A, B offers better value.
The trade-off is…
On balance, I'd go with…

vocabulary.gloss: what you give up for a gain
good value for money
similar enough to compare
very small

examples.label: Simple
examples.text: Option B is cheaper.

examples.label: With degree
examples.text: Option B is significantly cheaper, but slightly slower.

examples.label: Superlative
examples.text: Of the three suppliers, Vidal is the most reliable.

mistake.wrong: Option C is considerably the most reliable.
mistake.right: Option C is by far the most reliable.
mistake.why: 'Considerably', 'significantly' and 'much' modify comparatives ('considerably cheaper'). Superlatives take 'by far' or 'easily'.

guides.tip: Add the size of the difference: 'slightly', 'significantly', 'marginally'. It is what turns a comparison into a recommendation.

guides.title: Describing charts and trends
guides.explanation: Describing data means naming the direction, the size and the period. Never reading every number aloud. The same phrases work in a meeting and in IELTS Writing Task 1.
expressions: Sales rose sharply between January and March.
There was a steady decline in Q3.
Figures remained stable at around 12%.
The number of users doubled.
X peaked at 40,000 in June.
Overall, the trend is upward.

vocabulary.gloss: to go up
to go down
to stop changing
to reach the highest point
how fast it changed

vocabulary.term: a fifth / a quarter / a third
vocabulary.gloss: proportions

examples.label: Listing numbers
examples.text: In January it was 100, in February 120, in March 145…

examples.label: Describing
examples.text: Sales increased steadily over the first quarter, from 100 to 145.

examples.label: Overview
examples.text: Overall, both regions grew, though Spain grew far faster.

mistake.wrong: The sales augmented of 20%.
mistake.right: Sales increased by 20%.
mistake.why: Increase BY an amount of change; increase TO a final figure.

guides.tip: Always open with one sentence of overview before any detail. In IELTS Task 1 this sentence carries a large part of the mark.

guides.title: Days, times and deadlines
guides.explanation: Small words matter with dates and times. 'By Friday' means 'on Friday or before'. 'Until 6' means 'all the time up to 6'. Use 'on' for days and 'at' for clock times.
expressions: Please send it by Friday. (Friday or before)
I'm in the office until six. (all the time up to six)
The meeting is on Monday at ten.
The report is two days late.
Can we move the meeting to Thursday?

vocabulary.gloss: the last day or time to finish
after the right time
at the right time, not late
to change the day or time of something

examples.label: Deadline
examples.text: Could you reply by Friday?

examples.label: Up to a time
examples.text: I'm at my desk until five.

examples.label: Day and time
examples.text: The call is on Tuesday at 3 p.m.

mistake.wrong: I will finish it until Friday.
mistake.right: I will finish it by Friday.
mistake.why: Finishing happens at one moment, so use 'by'. Use 'until' for things that continue.

guides.tip: Give a day and a time: 'Thursday at 5 p.m.' is clearer than 'Thursday'.

guides.title: Core workplace vocabulary
guides.explanation: A small group of common words is enough for most work emails and conversations. Learn the words for people, places and tasks at work, and for simple business travel.
expressions: I work in the sales department.
I'm responsible for the invoices.
My manager is Elena.
I have a meeting at ten.
I'm on a business trip next week.
Could you book a hotel for me?

vocabulary.gloss: a person you work with
the person who leads your work
a part of a company, like Sales or Finance
a person or company that buys from you
a piece of work you must do
a journey for work
to reserve a room, a hotel or a ticket
strong verbs: to lead something / to make it better

examples.label: Weak verbs
examples.text: I did the project and made it better.

examples.label: Strong verbs
examples.text: I managed the project and improved the process.

examples.label: Job words
examples.text: My manager asked me to book the hotel.

mistake.wrong: My responsable asked me…
mistake.right: My manager asked me…
mistake.why: 'Responsable' is Spanish. In English, 'responsible' is an adjective: 'I'm responsible for the budget'.

guides.tip: Learn words in groups: people (manager, colleague), places (office, department), actions (book, check, send).

guides.title: Interview language
guides.explanation: Interview answers follow a shape: situation, what you did, what resulted. The result is the part most candidates leave out, and the only part the interviewer is listening for.
expressions: I have six years' experience in…
One of my strengths is…
I tend to be…
I would describe myself as…
In my last role, I was responsible for…
As a result, we…
Something I'm actively working on is…

vocabulary.gloss: your history and training
what you do well / need to improve
in charge of
something you succeeded in doing
wanting to succeed and progress
able to be trusted
sure about yourself
to have a good relationship with

examples.label: No result
examples.text: I was responsible for the social media accounts.

examples.label: With result
examples.text: I was responsible for the social media accounts, and over eighteen months I grew engagement by about 40%.

examples.label: Weakness, answered well
examples.text: I used to take on too much myself. I've been deliberately delegating more, and last quarter I handed over two full projects.

mistake.wrong: I have 6 years experience like project manager.
mistake.right: I have six years' experience as a project manager.
mistake.why: 'As' for a role; 'like' means 'similar to'. And note the apostrophe in 'years' experience'.

guides.tip: Every answer should end with a number, a result, or a lesson. Never end on the task itself.

guides.title: Reading strategies
guides.explanation: Professional reading is selective. Skim for structure first, then scan for the specific detail you need. Read every word only when the text is short and the stakes are high.
expressions: The main point is…
The writer suggests that…
According to the text…
This implies that…
The text doesn't say…

vocabulary.gloss: to read fast for the general idea
to search for a specific detail
to work out what is not stated
what is suggested but not said
to say the same thing in other words

examples.label: Stated
examples.text: Technology has changed the way we communicate.

examples.label: Implied
examples.text: Some experts argue people spend less time face to face — the writer is concerned, not neutral.

mistake.wrong: Answering from what you already believe about the topic.
mistake.right: Answering only from what the text actually says.
mistake.why: The most common reading error at B1–B2 is importing outside knowledge.

guides.tip: Find the answer, then find the exact line that proves it. If you cannot point at the line, you have guessed.

guides.title: IELTS Reading: True / False / Not Given
guides.explanation: IELTS Academic Reading gives you three passages and 40 questions in 60 minutes. Roughly 20 minutes per passage, with no extra transfer time. True/False/Not Given is the question type that trips up strong readers, because it tests only what is on the page.
expressions: TRUE — the text states this, in different words.
FALSE — the text states the opposite.
NOT GIVEN — the text does not say, either way.

vocabulary.gloss: the information is absent, not wrong
to state the opposite
something stated as true
words like 'all', 'some', 'never' that change meaning

examples.label: Text
examples.text: Many companies have introduced hybrid working since 2020.

examples.label: Statement → FALSE
examples.text: No companies introduced hybrid working after 2020.

examples.label: Statement → NOT GIVEN
examples.text: Hybrid working has improved productivity.

mistake.wrong: Marking something FALSE because you cannot find it.
mistake.right: Marking it NOT GIVEN.
mistake.why: FALSE requires the text to actively contradict the statement. Absence of evidence is NOT GIVEN.

guides.tip: There is no negative marking in IELTS. Never leave a question blank. Watch qualifiers: 'all', 'only', 'never' turn true statements false.

guides.title: IELTS Speaking: long turn and discussion
guides.explanation: IELTS Speaking is 11–14 minutes in three parts: familiar questions, a long turn from a topic card with one minute of preparation, and an abstract discussion. Part 3 is where band 7 is won. It rewards developed, non-memorised opinion.
expressions: I'd like to talk about…
The main reason for this is…
For instance, …
On the whole, I'd say…
It depends on the situation — for example…
That's an interesting question. I'd say…

vocabulary.gloss: Part 2: speak alone for 1–2 minutes
to extend it with reasons and examples
the 0–9 scale used for each section
to avoid sounding absolute

examples.label: Underdeveloped
examples.text: Yes, remote work will be more common.

examples.label: Band-worthy
examples.text: I think it will, mainly because companies have seen it can work. That said, it depends on the sector — you can't run a hospital remotely. For office work, though, I'd expect hybrid to become the default.

mistake.wrong: Reciting a memorised answer.
mistake.right: Answering the actual question, with a real example.
mistake.why: Recent IELTS marking puts more weight on natural, non-memorised responses.

guides.tip: In the one minute of preparation, write four words, not sentences. Sentences make you read; words make you speak.

guides.title: IELTS Writing: Task 1 and Task 2
guides.explanation: IELTS Academic Writing is 60 minutes for two tasks. Task 1 (150+ words, ~20 min) describes visual data. Task 2 (250+ words, ~40 min) is an essay, and it counts for twice as much, so protect its time.
expressions: Task 1: The chart shows… / Overall, … / The most striking feature is…
Task 2: It is often argued that… / In my view… / One argument in favour is… / However, critics point out that… / In conclusion…

vocabulary.gloss: the one or two sentences summarising the whole chart
to be more important than
the opposing view
to support with evidence

examples.label: Task 1 overview
examples.text: Overall, both categories increased, though online sales grew far more sharply.

examples.label: Task 2 opening
examples.text: It is often argued that remote work damages collaboration. While there is some truth in this, I believe the benefits outweigh the drawbacks.

mistake.wrong: Giving your opinion in Task 1.
mistake.right: Describing only what the data shows.
mistake.why: Task 1 is description. Opinion belongs in Task 2 and is penalised in Task 1.

guides.tip: Task 2 is worth double. If you are running out of time, leave Task 1 short and finish the essay.

guides.title: Structuring what you say
guides.explanation: Under pressure, fluency comes from structure, not vocabulary. A short plan: point, reason, example, close. Lets you speak for two minutes without hesitating.
expressions: My main point is…
There are two reasons for this.
The first is… The second is…
For example, when we…
So overall, I'd say…

vocabulary.gloss: to tell the listener what is coming
words used while thinking
to add more detail
speaking smoothly without long pauses

examples.label: Unstructured
examples.text: Well, it's difficult, there are many things, it depends, for example many factors…

examples.label: Structured
examples.text: I'd extend the deadline, for two reasons. First, the data isn't complete. Second, a rushed version will cost us more later. For example, last quarter we rushed and spent three weeks fixing it.

mistake.wrong: Long silence while translating in your head.
mistake.right: A filler phrase: 'That's a good question — let me think for a second.'
mistake.why: Fillers buy thinking time and count as fluency. Silence does not.

guides.tip: Always give yourself a number: 'two reasons'. Once you say it, your brain will find the second one.

guides.title: Linking words: and, but, because, so
guides.explanation: Linking words join two ideas. Use 'and' to add, 'but' for a difference, 'because' for a reason, and 'so' for a result. To show the order of steps, use 'first' and 'then'. Use 'also' to add one more thing.
expressions: The office is small and quiet. (add)
The price is good, but the delivery is slow. (difference)
I'm late because my train was late. (reason)
My train was late, so I'm late. (result)
First, open the file. Then, check the numbers. (order)
We also need more paper. (one more thing)

vocabulary.gloss: adds another idea
shows a difference or a problem
gives the reason: why?
gives the result: what happens next?
adds one more thing; it goes before the main verb

examples.label: Reason
examples.text: The report is late because the data arrived on Friday.

examples.label: Result
examples.text: The data arrived on Friday, so the report is late.

examples.label: Difference
examples.text: The hotel is nice, but it's far from the office.

mistake.wrong: Because the train was late, so I missed the meeting.
mistake.right: Because the train was late, I missed the meeting. / The train was late, so I missed the meeting.
mistake.why: 'Because' and 'so' do the same job. Use one, not both.

guides.tip: Before you send an email, look for three short sentences in a row. Can 'and', 'but' or 'so' join two of them?

guides.title: Formal linking: whereas, provided that, nevertheless
guides.explanation: At B2 the question is no longer which linker means 'but', but which one says exactly what you mean. 'Nevertheless' concedes a point and continues; 'whereas' sets two facts side by side; 'provided that' makes a condition; 'given that' and 'in light of' introduce a fact you are reasoning from. In a formal email or report, the right linker does the work of a whole sentence.
expressions: Concession: nevertheless, nonetheless, that said, notwithstanding
Comparison: whereas, while, by contrast
Condition: provided that, as long as, unless
Reasoning from a known fact: given that, in light of, in view of
Result: consequently, as a result, hence
Adding: furthermore, in addition, moreover

vocabulary.gloss: despite what I just said; starts a new sentence and takes a comma
joins two contrasting facts in one sentence
only if; introduces a condition
because of a fact both sides know; 'in light of' takes a noun
very formal 'despite'; takes a noun
as a result; starts a sentence or follows a semicolon

examples.label: Concession
examples.text: The pilot was expensive. Nevertheless, it paid for itself within a year.

examples.label: Comparison
examples.text: Vendor A offers phone support, whereas Vendor B offers email only.

examples.label: Condition
examples.text: We can hold this price provided that the order is confirmed by Friday.

examples.label: Known fact
examples.text: In light of last year's delays, we recommend a second supplier.

mistake.wrong: Nevertheless the price, we accepted the offer.
mistake.right: Despite the price, we accepted the offer. / The price was high. Nevertheless, we accepted the offer.
mistake.why: 'Nevertheless' links two sentences. Before a noun, use 'despite' or 'notwithstanding'.

guides.tip: Test each linker with its meaning: 'provided that' = 'only if', 'given that' = 'because we know'. If the paraphrase makes nonsense, the linker is wrong.

guides.title: Kinds of books: genres
guides.explanation: A genre is a kind of literature. The four big groups are stories (prose fiction), poetry, drama (plays) and non-fiction (true texts). To name a genre, look at the form: paragraphs, lines and stanzas, or dialogue with character names.
expressions: It's a novel about a family in Lagos.
It's a collection of short stories.
It's a book of poems.
It's a play in three acts.
It's a true story: a biography of Marie Curie.
It's written for children.

vocabulary.gloss: a long story, written in prose
a short story you can read in one go
a text written in lines, often with rhythm or rhyme
a story written for actors, with dialogue
the true story of another person's life
the true story of the writer's own life
a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson

examples.label: Form
examples.text: It has lines and stanzas, so it's a poem.

examples.label: Form
examples.text: It has character names and stage directions, so it's a play.

examples.label: Purpose
examples.text: It tells the true story of the writer's life, so it's an autobiography.

mistake.wrong: I'm reading a romance of Isabel Allende.
mistake.right: I'm reading a novel by Isabel Allende.
mistake.why: A long story is a 'novel'. 'Romance' means a love story. And a book is 'by' its writer, not 'of'.

guides.tip: Not sure? Ask two questions: is it true or invented? Is it in paragraphs, lines or dialogue?

guides.title: Parts of a story
guides.explanation: Most stories have the same parts. The characters are the people in the story. The setting is where and when it happens. The plot is what happens: a beginning, a problem (the conflict), the most exciting moment (the climax) and an ending.
expressions: The story takes place in Paris in 1920.
The main character is a young doctor.
At the beginning, she moves to a new city.
The problem is that nobody trusts her.
In the end, she saves the village.
It's told in the first person.

vocabulary.gloss: a person (or animal) in a story
the most important character; also 'protagonist'
the place and time of the story
the events of the story, in order
the problem or fight in the story
the most exciting moment, the turning point
the voice that tells the story

examples.label: Setting
examples.text: The story takes place on a small island in winter.

examples.label: Conflict
examples.text: The problem is that the boat can't leave because of the storm.

examples.label: Narrator
examples.text: 'I opened the door' — a first-person narrator.

mistake.wrong: The story happens in Lisbon. The argument is about a chef.
mistake.right: The story takes place in Lisbon. The plot is about a chef.
mistake.why: 'Argument' is a false friend: in English it means a fight. The events of a story are the 'plot'.

guides.tip: When you talk about a story, use the present simple: 'At the beginning, she moves to Lisbon.'

guides.title: Figurative language
guides.explanation: Figurative language uses words in a non-literal way to create a picture or a feeling. A simile compares with 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor says one thing IS another. Personification gives human qualities to things. Hyperbole exaggerates; understatement makes something sound smaller than it is.
expressions: The writer compares the city to a sleeping animal.
This simile makes the voice sound soft.
The wind is personified: it 'whispers'.
It's an exaggeration for effect.
The metaphor suggests that time steals from us.
It creates a calm, quiet mood.

vocabulary.gloss: a comparison with 'like' or 'as': 'her voice was like velvet'
describes one thing as another: 'time is a thief'
human qualities for non-human things: 'the wind whispered'
deliberate exaggeration: 'I've told you a million times'
making something serious sound small: 'just a scratch'
two opposite words together: 'deafening silence'
language that appeals to the senses

examples.label: Simile
examples.text: The office was as quiet as a library.

examples.label: Metaphor
examples.text: My inbox is a battlefield.

examples.label: Personification
examples.text: The old printer groaned and refused to work.

mistake.wrong: 'Her smile was like sunshine' is a metaphor.
mistake.right: 'Her smile was like sunshine' is a simile.
mistake.why: If you see 'like' or 'as', it's a simile. A metaphor has no comparison word: 'Her smile was sunshine.'

guides.tip: Never just name the device. Say what it does: 'This simile makes the room feel cold and empty.'

guides.title: Sound and form in poems
guides.explanation: Poems are built from lines, grouped into stanzas. Sound devices repeat sounds: alliteration repeats the first consonant ('wild and windy weather'), assonance repeats vowel sounds, rhyme matches end sounds. Free verse has no fixed rhyme or rhythm. Enjambment is when a sentence runs on past the end of a line.
expressions: The poem has two stanzas of five lines.
The rhyme scheme is ABAB.
The 'v' sound is repeated in 'vacant, vast'.
The sentence runs on into the next line.
It's written in free verse.
The repetition sounds like a heartbeat.

vocabulary.gloss: one row of words in a poem
a group of lines, like a paragraph in a poem
the same first consonant sound in nearby words
the same vowel sound in nearby words: 'go slow over the road'
the pattern of end rhymes, shown with letters: ABAB
a sentence that continues past the end of a line
poetry with no fixed rhyme scheme or metre

examples.label: Alliteration
examples.text: 'vacant, vast' (Whitman)

examples.label: Repetition
examples.text: 'filament, filament, filament' (Whitman)

examples.label: Couplet
examples.text: The last two lines of a Shakespeare sonnet rhyme: 'see / thee'.

mistake.wrong: The poem has three verses.
mistake.right: The poem has three stanzas.
mistake.why: In English, a group of lines is a 'stanza'. 'Verse' usually means poetry in general, or one line.

guides.tip: Read the poem aloud. Your ear finds alliteration and rhyme faster than your eyes.

guides.title: Device, evidence, effect
guides.explanation: Analysis is not naming techniques; it is explaining what they do. A strong analytical sentence has three parts: the device, a short quotation as evidence, and the effect on the reader or the meaning. Write about 'the speaker' or 'the narrator', not the poet, and use the present tense.
expressions: Whitman uses epizeuxis ('filament, filament, filament') to…
The repetition imitates…, which suggests…
This creates a sense of…
The image of… conveys…
The speaker's tone shifts from… to…
This could also be read as…

vocabulary.gloss: the voice in a poem; not necessarily the poet
to communicate a feeling or idea
to bring a feeling or image to mind
to make something stand out
the associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning
speaking directly to an absent person, thing or idea: 'O my soul'
allowing more than one plausible meaning

examples.label: Observation only
examples.text: There is a metaphor in line 7.

examples.label: Analysis
examples.text: The metaphor 'oceans of space' makes the universe feel deep and dangerous, so the soul's 'bridge' seems all the more fragile.

examples.label: Alternative reading
examples.text: 'Heaven made both, impossible' could also be read as bitter rather than resigned.

mistake.wrong: Dickinson felt very sad because her friend died.
mistake.right: The speaker's flat final lines suggest a grief too deep for open lament.
mistake.why: Don't treat the speaker as the poet, and don't guess at the poet's life. Analyse what the words on the page do.

guides.tip: Use the formula Device + Evidence + Effect. If you can't finish the sentence with 'which…', you've only made an observation.

guides.title: Irony, symbol and tone
guides.explanation: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or happens. In dramatic irony, the reader knows something a character doesn't. A symbol is an object or image that suggests a larger meaning; a motif is a detail that keeps returning. Tone is the speaker's attitude; mood is the atmosphere the reader feels.
expressions: The irony lies in the gap between… and…
The reader knows what the character doesn't.
The locked door recurs as a motif.
The thread can be read as a symbol of connection.
The tone is nostalgic, then abruptly flat.
Death is never named: it is only 'the Grave'.

vocabulary.gloss: when the audience knows something a character does not
when the outcome is the opposite of what was expected
something that suggests a meaning beyond itself
a recurring image, phrase or idea
the speaker's or narrator's attitude to the subject
the atmosphere created for the reader
a softer word for something harsh: 'passed away'

examples.label: Situational irony
examples.text: The girls who 'handled Destinies' cannot keep a promise for one night.

examples.label: Tone vs mood
examples.text: The narrator's tone is cheerful, but the mood is uneasy, because we know the storm is coming.

examples.label: Euphemism
examples.text: 'the Grave' and 'Heaven' stand in for death, which is never named.

mistake.wrong: The mood of the narrator is sarcastic.
mistake.right: The narrator's tone is sarcastic.
mistake.why: Tone belongs to the speaker or narrator. Mood belongs to the reader's experience of the text.

guides.tip: Irony needs two things side by side. Name both halves: what was said or expected, and what is meant or happens.
